# Age Perception

This section focuses on the perception of old age to determine at what point
a person is identified as old with respect to the respondents own age. I wish to 
answer Research Question 1: What is the correlation, if any, between an IT 
worker’s own age and the age at which they feel a person is deemed “old”.

```{r}
#| label: set-ap-Setup
#| echo: false
#| include: false

library('tidyverse')
library('ggthemes')
library('mice')

source("_graph_standards_bar.R")
source("_graph_standards_line.R")
source("_graph_standards_heatmap.R")
source("_graph_standards_scatter.R")

main_df <- readRDS("main_df.rds")
```

## Vector Definitions

I define the named and character vectors here to assign the labels in the survey 
with numbers so we can perform statistical analysis on the results along with
definitions to better understand data.

```{r}
#| label: vec-ap-VectorDefinitions}
# Map for converting Age_Perception section answers to Likert scale numbers.
age_perception_map <- c(
  "Very Young"  = 1, 
  "Young"       = 2, 
  "Middle Aged" = 3,
  "Old"         = 4, 
  "Very Old"    = 5
)

# Map of the Respondent Age Levels based on the Survey
# Note: All respondents under 18 have been removed.
respondent_age_levels <- c(
  "18-24 years old",
  "25-34 years old",
  "35-44 years old",
  "45-54 years old",
  "55-64 years old",
  "65+ years old"
)

# Map for better formatting of labels.
respondent_age_labels <- c(
  "18-24",
  "25-34",
  "35-44",
  "45-54",
  "55-64",
  "65+"
)

# Age Labels for Questions
age_labels <- c(
  "18-21", 
  "22-25", 
  "26-30", 
  "31-35", 
  "36-40",
  "41-45", 
  "46-50", 
  "51-55", 
  "56-60", 
  "61-65",
  "66-70", 
  "71-75", 
  "76-80", 
  "81+"
)

# Rating Labels
rating_labels = c(
  '1 - Very\nYoung', 
  '2 - Young', 
  '3 - Middle\nAged',
  '4 - Old', 
  '5 - Very\nOld'
)

```

## Age Perception dataframe

I create an Age Perception data frame with ID and answers to the Ageism 
Perception questions. 

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-ForwardFill

# Build data frame with only the variables that are valuable in this analysis.
age_perception_df <- main_df |>
  select(ID, Age, starts_with("Age_Perception_"))

# Factor Age and Map the Perception to a Number. 
age_perception_df <- age_perception_df |>
  mutate(
    respondent_age = factor(
      respondent_age_labels[match(Age, respondent_age_levels)],
      levels = respondent_age_labels
    ),
    across(starts_with("Age_Perception_"),
           ~ age_perception_map[.x])) 

# Drop Age Column in favor of respondent_age
age_perception_df <- age_perception_df |>
  select(-Age)
```

## Inspect Rows With Missing Values

There will be two strategies used to address NA values. If a row doesn't start
with NA, I can make logical determinations as to what the values would be with
a forward fill strategy. If the row starts with NA, I make a decision between
using an imputation strategy or dropping the row completely.

Before making these decisions, I want to see which respondents have any NAs 
across the Age_Perception items, how many NAs each has, and specifically how 
many begin with an NA in the first item.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-InspectNAs

na_inspect <- age_perception_df |>
  mutate(
    na_count   = rowSums(is.na(across(starts_with("Age_Perception_")))),
    starts_na  = is.na(Age_Perception_1)
  ) |>
  filter(na_count > 0) |>
  select(ID, respondent_age, na_count, starts_na)

na_inspect |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ID", 
                             "Respondent Age", 
                             "Num Missing",
                             "Starts With NA"))
```

- Rows with any NA: `r nrow(na_inspect)`
- Rows starting with NA (leading NA, unfixable by forward fill):
  `r sum(na_inspect$starts_na)`

## Dropping Rows

There is a fairly significant cutoff seen in the data. There are only 7 rows 
with missing data at all, and the rows with 9, 10, and 13 missing values
represent significant missing values. I choose to drop these completely.

```{r}
age_perception_df <- age_perception_df |>
  mutate(
    na_count   = rowSums(is.na(across(starts_with("Age_Perception_"))))
  )|>
  filter(na_count < 9 ) |>
  select(-na_count)

```

## Forward Fill

I use tidyr to fill in the missing values with the previously recorded value. 

The reasoning behind filling with previous numbers is the nature of the 
question. If a blank exists in the results, we can imply the previous value is 
correct. Only when the survey participant changes their answer does the next 
value take place.

For example:

`1 1 1 X 2 2 3`

In this example, we can assume X to be 1.

`1 2 2 3 X X 4`

In this example, we can assume X to be 3.

```{r}
age_perception_df <- age_perception_df |>
  # Reshape the Age_Perception columns to long format
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Age_Perception_"),
    names_to = "item",
    values_to = "response"
  ) |>
  # Group by survey taker
  group_by(ID) |>
  # Forward fill missing values within each respondent
  fill(response, .direction = "down") |>
  # Reshape back to wide format
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = item,
    values_from = response
  )
```

## Address NA Starts

To address rows that start with NA, I use MICE to impute the missing values.

Note: This analysis only averages the values of the 5 MICE iterations. Since all 
downstream analysis against this data uses Spearman or Kruskal-Wallis rank-based 
tests which depend only on value ordering rather than exact magnitudes, 
averaging is appropriate even when imputation uncertainty exists. Combined with 
sparse missing data (confined to a small number of leading NAs in a 14-item 
sequence) and a focus on central tendency rather than precise confidence 
intervals, this approach is a deliberate choice that balances rigor with 
simplicity for exploratory analysis.

I create a method vector to tell MICE not to use the ID column as a predictor. 
It will never be NA, so I don't need to worry about being imputed itself.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-CreatePredictorMatrix}

pred <- make.predictorMatrix(age_perception_df)
pred[,"ID"] <- 0
pred[, "respondent_age"] <- 0
```

## Run mice with 5 Iterations

I run MICE to create 5 iterations of analysis where missing items are filled.
I specify a seed so I can always be given matching results.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-MICEAnalysis
#| output: false
#| include: true

imputed <- mice(age_perception_df, 
                method = "pmm", 
                predictorMatrix = pred,
                m = 5, 
                seed = 53421)
```

## Extract the completed data back into our age_perception dataframe.

Here I take values from the MICE iterations and replace the NA values with the 
averaged predictions.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-AddMICEResults

age_perception_df <- complete(imputed, "long") |>
  group_by(.id) |>
  summarise(
    ID = first(ID),
    respondent_age = first(respondent_age),
    across(starts_with("Age_Perception_"), ~ round(mean(.x)))
  ) |>
  select(-'.id')

```

## Post Data Frame Manipulation Information:

Any NAs in age perception data frame: ***`r anyNA(age_perception_df)`***

Number of Research Participants for Age Perception Analysis is: 
***`r nrow(age_perception_df)`***

## Save Out Age Perception Data Frame
We will be using this cleaned data frame in our Correlation Analysis.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-SaveDataFrame

saveRDS(age_perception_df, 
        "age_perception_df.rds")
```

## Create Pivot Of Data Frame

I pivot the data frame in a format where I can group by the different age
groupings.


```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-ReshapeDataFrame

# Reshape to long format
df_long <- age_perception_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Age_Perception_"),
    names_to = "group",
    values_to = "rating"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    group_num = as.integer(str_extract(group, "\\d+")),
    age_group = factor(age_labels[group_num], levels = age_labels)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(rating))
```

## Build Summary Dataframe

Build summary data frame for analysis and graphing.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-SummaryDataFrame

df_summary <- df_long |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(
    mean_score = mean(rating),
  )
```

## Participant Average Age Perception Data

This graph shows the average score for all survey participants with respect to
the presented age group and their age scale rating. This is an expected 
semi-linear line that increases as the age group being presented increases.

Important Note: This does not take into consideration the participants own age.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ap-PerceptionGraph
#| fig-cap: "At What Age Is Old?"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 4

graph_line_chart(df_summary, 
                'age_group',
                'mean_score',
                'Age Group Being Rated', 
                'Age Scale Rating',
                y_breaks = 1:5,
                y_labels = rating_labels,
                y_limits = c(1,5))
```

## Heatmap of Respondents

This heatmap gives a better understanding of how each respondent rated the 
age group. From it there is the same somewhat linear grouping of most
of the respondents, however there are some outliers exposed by this graph.

Again, this graph does not take into consideration the participants own age.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ap-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Heatmap of Distribution of Age Perception Ratings"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 4

graph_heatmap(
  df          = df_long,
  x_category  = "age_group",
  y_category  = "rating",
  x_label     = "Age Group Being Rated",
  y_label     = "Age Scale Rating",
  y_labels    = rating_labels
)
```

## Age Group Counts

Again, it is important to reiterate the number of people represented in each of
the age groups. Because the respondents in the 18-24, 25-34 and 65+ were much
smaller than the other age groups, the following analysis of age based results
must be interpreted with caution.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ap-AgeGroupCounts
#| tbl-cap: Number of Participants by Age Group

age_perception_df |>
  count(respondent_age, name = "Count") |>
  mutate(Percentage = round(Count / sum(Count) * 100, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Age Group", "N", "%"))
```

## Age Perception based on own age

These graphs show how each age group rated the age groupings. The number of
respondents in the 18-24 range, 25-34 range, and 65+ range were limited which
introduces a larger confidence interval in their graphs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ap-LineChart
#| fig-cap: |
#|  Perception of Age by Respondent's Own Age<br>
#|  Each panel shows how that age group rated the 5 age brackets<br>
#|  Shaded band = 95% Confidence Interval
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 8
#| warning: false

df_summary <- df_long |>
  filter(!is.na(respondent_age)) |>
  group_by(respondent_age, age_group) |>
  summarise(
    mean_score = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    se         = sd(rating, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    ci_lo      = mean_score - 1.96 * se,
    ci_hi      = mean_score + 1.96 * se,
    .groups    = "drop"
  )

graph_line_chart(
  df          = df_summary,
  x_category  = "age_group",
  y_category  = "mean_score",
  x_label     = "Age Bracket Being Rated",
  y_label     = "Mean Perception Score",
  subtitle    = paste0(
    ""),
  facet_var   = "respondent_age",
  ci_lo       = "ci_lo",
  ci_hi       = "ci_hi",
  y_limits    = c(1, 5),
  y_breaks    = 1:5,
  y_labels    = rating_labels
)
```

## Overlaid Line Chart: Perception of "Old" by Respondent Age

I take the previous graphs and overlay them into one graph so it is easier to 
see how the age groups compare to each other.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ap-OverlayChart
#| fig-cap: |
#|  Overlay of Repondents Perception of Age by Age Group<br>
#|  Lines show mean perception score across 14 age brackets and shaded bands 
#|  represent 95% confidence interval
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| warning: false

graph_line_chart(
  df          = df_summary,
  x_category  = "age_group",
  y_category  = "mean_score",
  x_label     = "Age Bracket Being Rated",
  y_label     = "Mean Perception Score",
  color_var   = "respondent_age",
  ci_lo       = "ci_lo",
  ci_hi       = "ci_hi",
  y_limits    = c(1, 5),
  y_breaks    = 1:5,
  y_labels    = rating_labels
)
```

# How the groups responded by the numbers

The below table breaks down the survey taker's own age group and how they rated 
each of the other age groups in terms of old. with the following age labels
and their values:

* 1 - Very Young
* 2 - Young
* 3 - Middle Age
* 4 - Old
* 5 - Very Old


```{r}
#| label: tbl-ap-AgeTable
#| tbl-cap: "Ratings of Each Age Group by Respondents Own Age Group"
#| out-width: "100%"
df_summary |>
  mutate(mean_score = round(mean_score, 2)) |>
  select(respondent_age, age_group, mean_score) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from  = respondent_age,
    values_from = mean_score
  ) |>
  rename("Age Group Rated" = age_group) |>
  knitr::kable()
```


## "Old" Threshold by Respondent Age Group

To directly address my first Research Question, the following analysis 
identifies the first age bracket each respondent rates as "Old" (score ≥ 4) 
and summarizes those thresholds by the respondent's own age group. If a person's 
own age influences their perception of oldness, we would expect older 
respondents to set that threshold later than younger ones.

I build the threshold data frame to hold the information for the analysis and 
pivot the group by ratings.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-ThresholdCompute

threshold_df <- age_perception_df |>
  # Reshape from wide (One Column per age bracket) to long (one row per rating)
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = starts_with("Age_Perception_"),
    names_to  = "item",         # Ex: Age_Perception_4
    values_to = "rating"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    rating      = as.numeric(rating),
    # Grab the trailing number from the column name to help us sort the results
    # based on the age.
    group_num   = as.integer(str_extract(item, "\\d+")),
    #Map position to human-readable label.
    age_bracket = factor(age_labels[group_num], levels = age_labels)
  ) |>
  # Drop NA Rows or rating is out of allowable numbers
  filter(!is.na(respondent_age), rating >= 4) |>
  # For each survey participant, keep the row with the lowest group_numb that is 
  # still labeled as 'old'.
  group_by(ID, respondent_age) |>
  slice_min(group_num, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

# Afterword, we summarize the data by grouping by the respondent age group and
# finding the average threshold of the determination of an age being 'old'.

threshold_summary <- threshold_df |>
  group_by(respondent_age) |>
  summarise(
    n          = n(),                   # Number of participants in this group
    median_num = median(group_num),     # Median threshold
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Round median to nearest integer for consistent 
  # y-axis positioning and labeling.
  mutate(
    median_num = round(median_num),
    median_label = age_labels[median_num]
  )
```

## Age Threshold Chart

Here I graph the data that I previously built.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ap-ThresholdOutput
#| fig-cap: |
#|  Threshold of 'Old' by Age<br>
#|  Median first age bracket rated ≥ 4 (Old) by respondent age group
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

threshold_summary <- threshold_summary |>
  mutate(n_label = paste0("n=", n))

graph_bar_chart(
  df               = threshold_summary,
  x_category       = "respondent_age",
  y_category       = "median_num",
  label_col        = "median_label",
  inside_label_col = "n_label",
  x_label          = "Respondent Age Group",
  y_label          = "First Age Bracket Rated 'Old'",
  horizontal       = FALSE,
  y_limits         = c(0, 14),
  y_breaks         = 1:14,
  y_labels         = age_labels
)
```

Respondents in the 35–44 age group set the "old" threshold at **56–60**, while 
all other groups converge on **61–65**. The direction is consistent with what 
Research Question 1 would predict — younger respondents label "old" slightly 
earlier — though the difference is modest (one age bracket). Note that the 18–24 
and 25–34 groups have very small sample sizes (n=2 and n=7 respectively), so 
those results should be interpreted with caution. 

Further investigation is performed during Correlation Analysis.

## Individual Threshold Scatter Plot

The bar chart above summarizes each age group down to a single median
threshold, which can obscure how much individual respondents actually vary.
The scatter plot below shows every respondent's own individual threshold
(the first age bracket they rated "Old") against their own age group, with a
loess trend line to visualize the overall direction of the relationship. Both
variables are ordinal with a limited number of levels, so points are jittered
slightly to keep overlapping respondents visible.

Because a straight linear regression line would imply a linear relationship
between two ordinal variables — an assumption not required for the Spearman
correlation used to test Research Question 1 — a loess smoother is used here
instead, purely as a visual aid rather than a fitted statistical model.

Statistical analysis will be undertaken in the Correlation section.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ap-ScatterPrep

threshold_scatter_df <- threshold_df |>
  mutate(
    # Numeric position of the respondent's own age group (1 = 18-24 ... 6 = 65+)
    respondent_age_num = as.integer(respondent_age),
    # Small jitter so overlapping respondents remain visible
    respondent_age_jit = jitter(respondent_age_num, amount = 0.15),
    group_num_jit       = jitter(group_num, amount = 0.3),
    # Add age bracket label for Y-axis
    group_label = age_labels[group_num]
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ap-ThresholdScatter
#| fig-cap: |
#|  Individual "Old" Threshold by Respondent Age (Jittered)<br>
#|  Each point is one respondent's first age bracket rated "Old" (≥ 4);
#|  dashed line is a loess trend, shown for visual reference only
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false

graph_scatter(
  df           = threshold_scatter_df,
  x_category   = "respondent_age_jit",
  y_category   = "group_num_jit",
  x_label      = "Respondent Age Group (1 = 18-24, 6 = 65+)",
  y_label      = "First Age Bracket Rated 'Old'",
  trend_line   = TRUE,
  trend_method = "loess",
  x_breaks     = 1:6,
  x_limits     = c(0.5, 6.5),
  y_breaks     = 1:14,
  y_labels     = age_labels
)
```

## Conclusion

Having limited participation from the 18-24 age group limits the ability to 
provide better analysis. The participation in the 25-35 and 65+ also leads to
caution in the interpretation of the results.

There is a strong linear relationship between the age scale rating and the age
group being rated.  I also start to see some visual elements that support 
Research Question 1 in the Individual Threshold Scatter Plot. Further 
correlation analysis is needed and performed in the Correlation section.
